kit/netgd — the Godot transport binding

9 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓

kit/netgd connects the engine-independent replication core and session to Godot’s SceneMultiplayer. It sends packets with send_bytes and receives them through peer_packet, using the installed MultiplayerPeer. gd.host / gd.join create native ENet peers; gd.webrtc_host / gd.webrtc_join handle browser room-code setup. The Steam adapter supplies another transport implementation.

Using SceneMultiplayer lets Kit share the engine’s multiplayer peer with @(gd_rpc), MultiplayerSpawner, and MultiplayerSynchronizer. Keep each session’s transport state in its owning script struct; the procedures receive that state explicitly.

Transport channels#

  • channel 0 remains available for Godot RPC and scene-replication traffic.
  • CHANNEL_RELIABLE (1) carries commands, results, transitions, chat, and join snapshots using RELIABLE delivery.
  • CHANNEL_STREAM (2) carries owner-state snapshots using UNRELIABLE_ORDERED. A later snapshot supersedes a lost sample.

With a Session_Wire attached, the session’s Send_Proc selects the channel and calls send_to, send_reliable, or send_stream. A custom Send_Proc must translate peer IDs through wire_engine_peer(to_peer) -> (engine_peer, ok). Do not cast ksess.Peer_Id directly to an engine integer: Kit’s BROADCAST_PEER is Peer_Id(-1), while Godot interprets raw -1 as “all except peer 1.” The adapter maps broadcast to engine 0 and returns ok = false for NO_PEER; discard a send with no connected destination.

Session_Wire and the four forwarding methods#

Session_Wire binds the session’s send procedure, packet routing, Godot connection signals, and client join handshake. The stock Boot contains it as boot.wire and attaches it during boot_attach. A game managing the components directly can keep its own wire field.

Godot signal receivers must be registered @(gd_method) procedures on a game script. For a script that directly owns ses and wire, the forwarding methods look like this:

Odin
@(gd_method)
cave_lobby_on_packet :: proc(self: ^CaveLobby, id: gd.Int, packet: gd.Packed_Byte_Array) {
	netgd.wire_receive(&self.wire, id, packet)
}

@(gd_method)
cave_lobby_on_peer_left :: proc(self: ^CaveLobby, id: gd.Int) {
	ksess.session_peer_disconnected(&self.ses, ksess.Peer_Id(id))
}

@(gd_method)
cave_lobby_on_net_up :: proc(self: ^CaveLobby) {
	ksess.session_client_join(&self.ses)
}

@(gd_method)
cave_lobby_on_net_down :: proc(self: ^CaveLobby) {
	ksess.session_peer_disconnected(&self.ses, ksess.HOST_PEER)
}

Attach them after the node enters the tree, normally in _ready, and pump the wire from _process:

Odin
netgd.wire_attach(&self.wire, self.owner, &self.ses, MSG_SESSION)
netgd.wire_listen(&self.wire, "on_packet", "on_peer_left", "on_net_up", "on_net_down")

// process():
netgd.wire_pump(&self.wire, now_s())

wire_attach installs the session’s send adapter. It survives session_host_start, session_client_start, and session_host_resume, so it need not be repeated for those transitions. wire_listen connects:

  • peer_packet to on_packet;
  • peer_disconnected to on_peer_left;
  • connected_to_server to on_net_up; and
  • both connection_failed and server_disconnected to on_net_down.

An empty method name skips that signal. Check the disconnect requirements before skipping one.

Hosting and joining#

The begin_* helpers open the selected transport and start its session:

Odin
// native (ENet) — the address is known before dialing
netgd.begin_host(&wire, port, name, max_peers = 32, token = 0) -> bool  // false = port taken
netgd.begin_join(&wire, addr, port, token, name) -> bool

// Browser WebRTC: the relay assigns the room code after connection.
netgd.begin_host_web(&wire, url, name, token = 0, room = "") -> bool  // false = relay socket refused
netgd.begin_join_web(&wire, url, room, token, name) -> bool
netgd.web_poll(&wire)   // every frame: pumps the signaling handshake
netgd.web_close(&wire)  // full teardown — retry a failed join, or an heir raising a new room

token identifies the local participant for reconnects. Hosting helpers pass the host’s token; joining helpers pass the joining player’s token. The session uses it to reclaim that participant’s identity after a handoff. For WebRTC, room requests a reserved room code. An empty value requests a new code. The hosting helper returns before the signaling relay assigns that code, so call web_poll each frame and read gd.webrtc_room_code(node) when available. Use gd.webrtc_session_state and gd.webrtc_error_reason to display progress or failure in the lobby.

Web host migration reserves a successor’s code before the handoff. The successor opens that reservation while other clients reconnect to it. Session logic, commands, and replication use the same interfaces after either transport is installed.

Boot provides the corresponding lobby operations: boot_host, boot_join, boot_host_web, and boot_join_web. The four begin_* helpers select a transport and call transport_host or transport_join. Use those generic procedures when a setting or retry policy chooses the provider at runtime; see Swapping transports.

Native ENet join codes#

Native join codes use the signaling relay as an endpoint directory. The host registers its bound port under a generated code. A joiner resolves the code to the host’s observed endpoint, then follows the normal begin_join flow. tests/webrtc/signal_server.mjs implements the reference native-room protocol; the production relay exposes it at /rtc.

A Boot-based game uses these operations, with <game>_net_frame driving the rendezvous state. The hosted code appears in lobby status and boot_room_code; a resolved join starts boot_join, and an invalid code returns to the menu with its reason:

Odin
// Host with a join code (kui.lobby_show_code reveals the stock
// lobby's code field, and kui.lobby_code reads what the human typed):
kboot.boot_host_coded(&self.boot, RELAY_URL, port, name)
// Join by code rather than supplying an address and port:
kboot.boot_join_code(&self.boot, RELAY_URL, "KWXP", token, name)

A custom lobby can drive code.odin directly:

Odin
// Host: call after begin_host(port) succeeds.
netgd.code_host_open(&rdv, RELAY_URL, port)
// Joiner: resolve a code to an address.
netgd.code_join_open(&rdv, RELAY_URL, "KWXP")

// both, every frame, until it resolves:
switch netgd.code_poll(&rdv, &wire) {
case .Ready:
    if rdv.is_host {show(netgd.code_room(&rdv))} // the code to share
    else {ip, port := netgd.code_endpoint(&rdv); begin_join(&wire, ip, port, token, name)}
case .Failed: // Show rdv.err: .No_Room, .Full, or .Closed.
              // Offer another configured transport if appropriate.
}

examples/hello_net exercises the Boot helpers against a local relay. Setting HELLO_RELAY enables its code-entry field. The supported cases include a same-LAN pair, a public or port-forwarded host, and common port-preserving NAT. The relay supplies each joiner’s observed endpoint and wire_punch sends UDP packets to establish the mapping.

Raw ENet has no TURN relay for symmetric NAT. Report connection failure and offer another configured transport, such as WebRTC with TURN or Steam; verify reachability for the deployment rather than assuming the alternative succeeds.

Disconnect handling#

Forward peer_disconnected so the session removes a disconnected client from its roster. Forward connection_failed so a refused join can leave the “Joining...” state. server_disconnected uses the same failure callback to report host loss.

Scriptgen checks literal method names passed to wire_listen, listen_packets, and Boot’s methods against registered @(gd_method) procedures. A misspelling is a build error; an empty string deliberately omits a connection.

Host migration#

The cooperative session selects a successor; netgd.Succession provides the connection information that lets survivors find it. Boot controls retry timing, timeouts, and reconnect orchestration. boot_migration installs the callbacks; live simulation-lane migration is not supported by this path. See session recovery.

A handoff record is [kind u8][payload], encoded and decoded by this package through succession_decode:

  • .Native_Addr carries [addr][port]: the successor’s address as observed by the host and a port derived from its seat. It requires an ENet peer-address lookup. A provider lacking that lookup cannot supply this handoff.
  • .Web_Room carries [code]: the pre-reserved relay room opened by the successor. Boot schedules reconnect attempts while that room becomes available.

Steam handoff is not implemented by these kinds. It needs a verified peer-ID lookup and a corresponding rendezvous encoding; a Steam lobby’s owner is not necessarily the successor chosen by the Kit session.

Configure Succession{kind, signal_url, base_port, token, name} once, normally through boot_succ_config. On Ev_Backup_Target, the host’s succession_torch publishes the handoff. The successor calls succession_raise; a survivor calls succession_dial for one connection attempt. Boot owns the retries. succession_named checks whether a successor is present. The game supplies its campaign backup, entity cleanup, and recovery UI through boot_migration callbacks.

wire_receive and the kind byte#

The low seven bits of the packet’s leading byte identify the game protocol installed with wire_attach. The high bit, 0x80, marks stream-channel traffic. wire_receive masks that bit before comparing the protocol ID with wire.kind. Custom routing must use the same mask so it recognizes both reliable and stream packets for the protocol. Route another raw-byte protocol before calling it. This lets several protocols share the same peer_packet signal without decoding each other’s packets.

Link simulation#

Odin
wire_set_latency :: proc(wire: ^Session_Wire, ms: int, jitter_ms := 0, loss_pct := 0, burst := 1, bandwidth_bps := 0)

wire_set_latency delays each packet on this peer’s receive path by the given one-way latency; 0 disables the delay. wire_pump later delivers buffered packets to the session. This happens above the transport, so it does not delay ENet’s own acknowledgements and retransmissions. The integration tests use 120 ms to check local prediction and delayed authority confirmation.

jitter_ms adds uniform extra delay in [0, jitter) while preserving FIFO order per sender. loss_pct drops selected stream batches, which later samples can supersede. For reliable traffic it instead adds retransmission delay, preserving the channel’s reliable-delivery requirement.

burst controls mean lost-run length in packets. At 1, losses are independent; larger values use a Gilbert-Elliott-style model that groups roughly ~burst losses between clean intervals at the same average rate. This tests whether an input-redundancy window survives a cluster of drops and how stacked reliable retransmission delays affect the game.

bandwidth_bps limits modeled receive throughput in bytes/s, shared by all senders. Excess packets queue and increase delay. Configure each endpoint’s receive model separately to test asymmetric links. The model cannot assign different conditions to individual senders on the same receiver.

Boot reads these settings from environment variables:

Shell
QD_LATENCY=120 QD_JITTER=30 QD_LOSS=3 ./run_two_windows.sh        # receive latency, jitter, and loss
QD_LOSS=3 QD_BURST=4 QD_BANDWIDTH=16000 ./run_two_windows.sh      # bursty loss with a 16KB/s receive budget

Traffic and link stats#

The wire counts framed bytes sent and received by session message kind: state, stream, command, spawn, and app. App traffic is also split by its tag byte, so simulation traffic can be identified separately. Read the completed one-second window with:

Odin
netgd.wire_traffic(&wire) -> string
// "rx 3.2k state 2.1 stream 0.8 app16 0.2 · tx 0.4k cmd 0.3"
netgd.wire_rates(&wire) -> Wire_Rates // packets/s and bytes/s, in/out
netgd.wire_link_quality(&wire, peer) -> (rtt_ms, jitter_ms, loss_pct, ok)

wire_traffic formats the netgraph traffic row; wire_rates returns aggregate packet and byte rates. Boot populates both. Compare these measurements when changing wire=f16, stream rates, or interest filtering.

wire_link_quality reads ENet’s per-peer smoothed RTT, RTT variance, and loss scaled by PACKET_LOSS_SCALE. A client asks about ksess.HOST_PEER; a host asks about a specific client. Quickdraw’s netgraph shows this integration.

Kicks: wire_drop#

A low-level kick first calls ksess.session_kick to remove the player and send SES_KICKED, then closes its transport connection. Closing immediately can discard the queued reason packet, causing the client to report host loss instead.

Odin
wire_drop :: proc(wire: ^Session_Wire, peer: ksess.Peer_Id, after := 0.75)

wire_drop schedules a deadline. wire_pump requests the disconnect after that deadline; it does not inspect acknowledgements before doing so. The delay gives the notification time to leave the reliable queue. The session has already removed the player from its connected roster. For a game managing the wire directly:

Odin
was, ok := ksess.session_kick(&self.ses, target, ban = true)
if !ok {return}
netgd.wire_drop(&self.wire, was) // deferred: the KICKED message flushes first

drop_peer(node, peer) requests the actual graceful disconnect through multiplayer_peer_disconnect_peer with force=false. Use boot_kick in a Boot-based game to perform both the session removal and the delayed wire close.

pba_view#

Odin
pba_view :: proc "contextless" (pba: ^gd.Packed_Byte_Array) -> []u8

pba_view borrows the Packed_Byte_Array contents without copying. Use that view only while the array remains alive, normally within the receiving method. Pass it to knet.reader_make and copy bytes retained after the callback. gd.packed_byte_array_view is the underlying engine helper; netgd.pba_view is its networking alias.

Without a Session_Wire, listen_packets(node, method) connects peer_packet to one registered @(gd_method) on the node’s script.

Swapping transports#

Transport describes provider-specific connection setup, pumping, teardown, statistics, and peer addressing. Session packets continue to use SceneMultiplayer’s raw-byte interface:

Odin
Transport :: struct {
    name:       string,           // "enet" / "webrtc" / "steam"
    rendezvous: Rendezvous_Kind,  // Handoff format supplied by address (.None = no migration)
    open_host:  proc(wire, at: Endpoint, name: string, token: u64, dedicated: bool) -> bool,
    open_join:  proc(wire, at: Endpoint, name: string, token: u64, spectate: bool) -> bool,
    pump:       proc(wire),       // nil = the engine polls it
    close:      proc(wire),       // nil = no extra resources to close
    link:       proc(wire, peer) -> (rtt_ms, jitter_ms, loss_pct: f64, ok: bool),
    address:    proc(wire, peer, allocator) -> (string, bool),
}

Endpoint :: struct {   // Connection details interpreted by the selected transport
    addr: cstring,     // native: the host's address (join) · web: the relay url
    port: int,         // native: the port to bind or dial
    room: cstring,     // web: the room code to reserve or join
    peer_id: u64,      // steam: the host's steam id (join)
    max_peers: int,    // host: seat cap (0 = the transport's default)
}

open_host and open_join are required. Optional callbacks have these effects:

slot nil means what the user sees
pump the engine polls it (ENet, Steam) no separate transport pump
close no extra resources outlive the peer no provider-specific teardown
link per-peer statistics are unavailable the netgraph leaves link values blank
address no peer rendezvous address is available .Native_Addr migration cannot name the successor; .Web_Room uses reserved room codes without this callback

transport_host and transport_join remember the chosen provider in the wire. transport_service, transport_close, wire_link_quality, and succession then use that provider’s callbacks. Generated <game>_net_frame calls the service pump through Boot. A peer installed directly with gd.host and wire_attach uses the ENet fallback; ENet-specific operations check the peer’s class and return ok = false for another type.

The supplied records are netgd.ENET, netgd.WEBRTC, and ksteam.TRANSPORT (Steam). Another provider fills the same record, with any rendezvous encoding required for migration. The session wire and signal-forwarding methods can keep the same interface.

A session uses one MultiplayerPeer provider for every seat. Select ENet, WebRTC, or Steam for the run; individual participants cannot mix providers within that session. A Steam user can host an ENet or WebRTC session for peers using that provider.

Related features have separate requirements:

  • LAN discovery is not supplied. A game can implement UDP discovery, or use the join-code relay for a same-LAN pair.
  • Server browsing is not supplied. It needs a directory service with registration, listing, and liveness; join codes only resolve a known room.
  • Splitscreen has one session identity per process. Local controller and camera handling belong to the game; Kit does not allocate independent local seats.
  • Consoles and platform-specific console transports are untested here.
